title: Data Structures and Algorithms Multiple Choice
description: Big-O complexity, two pointers/sliding window, BFS/DFS, cycle detection, and dynamic programming from module 05.

options.text: O(n)
O(n²)
O(log n)

questions.explanation: A loop nested inside another loop over the same input does roughly n * n work, which is O(n²) — work quadruples when n doubles.

questions.prompt: Binary search halves the remaining range on every iteration. What is its time complexity?

options.text: O(n)
O(n²)
O(log n)

questions.explanation: Halving the search range each step means the number of steps grows by only one when n doubles — that is the definition of O(log n).

questions.prompt: For `twoSum(sortedArr, target)` using the two-pointer technique on a SORTED array, what do you do when `sortedArr[left] + sortedArr[right] < target`?

options.text: Move `left` one step to the right to increase the sum
Move `right` one step to the left to decrease the sum
Restart both pointers from the ends
Swap `left` and `right`

questions.explanation: When the current sum is too small, the only way to increase it (on a sorted array) is to move the left pointer right, since every value from that point on is greater or equal.

questions.prompt: Why does the two-pointer / sliding window technique reduce a nested-loop O(n²) solution to O(n)?

options.text: Each pointer moves in only one direction and makes at most n moves total, so no pair or window is re-examined from scratch
It sorts the array first, which is always free
It uses recursion instead of loops, which is inherently faster
It only works on arrays with fewer than 100 elements

questions.explanation: Because each pointer only advances (never backtracks), the total work across the whole pass is bounded by n moves per pointer, giving O(n) instead of checking every pair.

options.text: BFS uses a FIFO queue (`shift`); DFS uses a LIFO stack (`pop`) — everything else is the same
BFS uses recursion; DFS never uses recursion
DFS always runs faster than BFS on the same graph
BFS cannot be used on graphs with cycles

questions.explanation: The only structural difference is FIFO (`queue.shift()`) for BFS versus LIFO (`stack.pop()`) for DFS. Both mark visited nodes and run in O(V + E).

questions.prompt: In an unweighted graph, which traversal is guaranteed to find the shortest path (fewest edges) from a start node?

options.text: BFS, because it explores level by level
DFS, because it explores as deep as possible first
Neither — both find arbitrary paths
Only Dijkstra's algorithm can do this

questions.explanation: BFS visits all direct neighbors before any of their neighbors (level by level), which is exactly why it finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

questions.prompt: Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm detects a cycle in a linked list using two pointers moving at different speeds. What is its space complexity, and why is that an advantage over a hash-set approach?

options.text: O(1) extra space, because it only tracks two pointers instead of storing every visited node
O(n) extra space, same as the hash-set approach
O(log n) extra space, because it halves the list each step
O(n²) extra space, because it compares every pair of nodes

questions.explanation: Floyd's algorithm trades the hash-set's O(n) memory for two pointers (`slow`/`fast`), achieving O(1) extra space while still running in O(n) time.

questions.prompt: What two properties must a problem have for dynamic programming to help?

options.text: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
A sorted input and a single loop
A graph structure and a queue
Recursion and no base case

questions.explanation: DP applies when the same smaller subproblem recurs (overlapping subproblems) and the best overall answer is built from the best answers to smaller pieces (optimal substructure).
